entries.short: A way for a model to build each output as a weighted average of inputs, where the weights say how relevant each input is to the current position.
Attention where queries, keys and values all come from the same sequence, so every token can look at every other token in one step.
entries.formula: Q = XW^Q, K = XW^K, V = XW^V

entries.short: Runs several attention operations (heads) in parallel on different learned projections, then concatenates and projects their outputs, so each head can focus on a different kind of relation.
Attention whose scores are dot products of queries and keys divided by √dₖ, which keeps the softmax from saturating when dₖ is large.
Attention where queries come from one sequence (e.g. the decoder) and keys and values from another (e.g. the encoder output).
The three roles in attention: a query is matched against keys to get weights, and those weights average the values.
Sets attention scores to −∞ for positions a token must not see (e.g. future tokens in a decoder), so they get zero weight after softmax.
A neural network built from stacked self-attention and feed-forward layers with residual connections and normalization, with no recurrence or convolution.
The part of a model that reads the input and turns it into a sequence of contextual representations.
The part of a model that generates the output one step at a time, conditioned on what it has produced so far and (often) on the encoder's output.
An architecture where an encoder maps the input to representations and a decoder generates the output from them; used for translation and summarization.
A learned vector that represents a discrete item such as a token; similar items end up with nearby vectors.
Information about each token's position added to its embedding, because attention by itself ignores order.
Adds a layer's input to its output, so the layer only has to learn a change; this makes very deep networks much easier to train.
Normalizes each example's features to zero mean and unit variance, then applies a learned scale and shift; stabilizes training independent of batch size.
Normalizes each feature using the mean and variance across the current mini-batch, then applies a learned scale and shift.
During training, randomly sets a fraction p of activations to zero (and rescales the rest) so the network cannot rely on any single unit; a regularizer.
entries.formula: y = m ⊙ x / (1 − p), m ~ Bernoulli(1 − p)

entries.short: Layers of linear maps with a nonlinearity in between, applied independently to each position.
entries.formula: FFN(x) = max(0, xW₁ + b₁) W₂ + b₂

entries.short: Turns a vector of scores into probabilities: exponentiate each score and divide by the sum, so outputs are positive and add up to 1.
A raw, unnormalized score a model outputs before softmax or sigmoid turns it into a probability.
The nonlinear function applied after a linear layer; without it a stack of layers would collapse into one linear map.
An activation that passes positive values unchanged and sets negative values to zero.
A smooth activation that weights its input by the probability a standard normal variable is below it; common in Transformers.
Squashes any real number into (0, 1); used for binary probabilities and gates.
Squashes any real number into (−1, 1); a zero-centred cousin of the sigmoid.
A network that reads a sequence one step at a time, carrying a hidden state forward; inherently sequential, which limits parallelism.
An RNN cell with input, forget and output gates and a separate cell state, which lets it keep information over long sequences.
A simpler gated RNN cell than the LSTM, with update and reset gates and no separate cell state.
A network that slides small learned filters over its input, sharing weights across positions; good at local patterns.
The internal vector a model keeps for a position or time step, summarizing what it has seen so far.
Computes the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight by applying the chain rule backwards through the network.
Repeatedly moves the parameters a small step against the gradient of the loss, which is the direction of steepest decrease.
Gradient descent using the gradient from a small random batch of examples at each step instead of the whole dataset.
An optimizer that keeps running averages of the gradient and its square to give each parameter its own adaptive step size.
How big a step the optimizer takes on each update; too high diverges, too low trains slowly.
Starting training with a small learning rate and increasing it over the first steps, which avoids unstable early updates.
Shrinks weights a little toward zero at every step, which discourages overly large weights and reduces overfitting.
Any technique that discourages a model from fitting noise in the training data, such as dropout, weight decay or label noise.
When a model fits the training data well but does worse on new data because it has memorized noise instead of general patterns.
The number training tries to minimize; it measures how wrong the model's predictions are.
The standard classification loss: the negative log of the probability the model gave to the correct answer.
Measures how much one probability distribution differs from a reference distribution; zero only when they are identical, and not symmetric.
The average of squared differences between predictions and targets; the usual regression loss.
A language-model metric: the exponential of the average per-token cross-entropy. Lower means the model is less surprised by the text.
entries.formula: PPL = exp(−(1/N) Σᵢ log p(xᵢ | x₍<ᵢ₎))

entries.short: A machine-translation metric that counts overlapping n-grams between the output and reference translations, with a brevity penalty.
A decoding method that keeps the k most likely partial outputs at each step instead of only the single best one.
The unit of text a model reads and writes, typically a word piece; text is split into tokens before being embedded.
A tokenization method that starts from characters and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair, giving a fixed vocabulary of subword units.
The fixed set of tokens a model knows; each token has its own embedding and output logit.
A model that assigns probabilities to text, usually by predicting the next token from the ones before it.
Generating a sequence one element at a time, where each new element is conditioned on everything generated so far.
Training a model on a large general dataset first, so it can later be adapted to specific tasks with much less data.
Continuing to train a pre-trained model on a smaller task-specific dataset.
Reusing what a model learned on one task or dataset to do better on another.
Fine-tunes a large model by freezing its weights and learning a small low-rank update for selected weight matrices.
entries.formula: W' = W + BA, rank(BA) = r ≪ d

entries.short: A setting chosen before training rather than learned, such as learning rate, batch size or number of layers.
How many examples are processed together to compute one gradient update.
One full pass of training over the whole training dataset.
Combining predictions from several models (e.g. by averaging), which is usually more accurate than any one of them.
Using a trained model to make predictions, as opposed to training it.
Similarity of two vectors measured by the cosine of the angle between them, ignoring their lengths.
A layer with many sub-networks (experts) where a learned router sends each token to only a few, adding capacity without adding much compute per token.
Training a small student model to match the output probabilities of a larger teacher model.
Storing weights or activations with fewer bits (e.g. 8- or 4-bit integers instead of 32-bit floats) to save memory and speed up inference.
A generative model trained to reverse a gradual noising process; it creates data by starting from noise and denoising step by step.
Two networks trained against each other: a generator makes fake samples and a discriminator tries to tell them from real ones.
An autoencoder whose encoder outputs a probability distribution over a latent space, trained with a reconstruction loss plus a KL term toward a simple prior.
Learns representations by pulling matching pairs (e.g. two views of one image) together and pushing non-matching pairs apart.
Learning by trial and error: an agent takes actions in an environment and adjusts its behaviour to maximize long-term reward.
When gradients shrink (or blow up) as they pass back through many layers or time steps, making early layers hard to train.
